sections.h2: What should an Indiana home seller know about the state itself?
sections.html:
Indiana covers 36,418 square miles, holds 92 counties, and is split into three quite different landscapes that shape the houses sold in them. The north and center sit on glacial till plains that are mostly flat with fertile soil, the northwest has sand ridges and dunes along Lake Michigan, and the south is hilly with exposed bedrock, limestone caves and quarries.

The state's highest point is Hoosier Hill in Wayne County at 1,257 feet, while the geographic center falls inside Marion County. The Wabash River is the official state river. A seller in a Lake Michigan dune town deals with different lots, soil and insurance questions than a seller on a limestone hillside near the Ohio River.

Manufacturing carries unusual weight here. Nearly 17 percent of Indiana's non-farm workers are in manufacturing, the highest share of any state, with motor vehicles, auto parts and pharmaceuticals among the leading exports. A plant closing or a new line can move demand for homes in a small county quickly, which is why local employer news matters when you price a house.

sections.h2: Which Indiana cities and counties are the largest?
sections.html:
Indianapolis is the largest city by a wide margin, and Marion County is the largest county. The 2020 census counted 887,642 people in Indianapolis, 253,617 in Fort Wayne, 117,429 in Evansville and 101,168 in South Bend. Indianapolis, Fort Wayne, Evansville and South Bend anchor the four largest metro areas, and the Indianapolis metro has more than two million residents.

Marion County has a consolidated city-county government. The table lists the ten most populous counties using 2025 estimates.

The county seat matters when you sell. Deeds are recorded with the county recorder, tax bills are paid to the county treasurer, and deduction applications go to the county auditor, all through county offices.

sections.h2: How is property tax run in Indiana?
sections.html:
Indiana splits the job among the county assessor, the county auditor, the county treasurer and the state Department of Local Government Finance (DLGF). The assessor sets the value, the auditor applies deductions and exemptions, DLGF turns local budgets into tax rates, and the treasurer collects.

  • Assessors value property by mass appraisal, comparing it with similar nearby properties and adjusting yearly using recent sales.
  • The Form 11 notice carries the assessed value, which DLGF calls the starting point for your annual payments.
  • To contest a value, contact the local assessor by June 15 of the year the Form 11 arrives. If no Form 11 is mailed, the deadline is June 15 of the next year.
  • The appeal path runs from Form 130 and an informal conference to the county Property Tax Assessment Board of Appeals, then the Indiana Board of Tax Review, then the Indiana Tax Court.

Bills are due in two installments, on May 10 and November 10. For 2026 DLGF lists May 11 and November 10. A payment up to 30 days late carries a 5 percent penalty when there is no back tax on the property, and a longer delay carries 10 percent. Unpaid taxes can lead to a tax sale, which is why a delinquent bill belongs near the top of any sale checklist.

The circuit breaker caps

Property classCap on gross assessed value
Homestead1%
Residential, long-term care, agricultural land2%
Nonresidential and personal property3%

Tax above the cap is removed through a credit, so a rental house is capped at a higher level than an owner-occupied home. The 1% cap applies only when the property receives the homestead standard deduction.

sections.h2: What does it take to transfer title and record a deed in Indiana?
sections.html:
A deed must be acknowledged before a notarial officer and must carry the grantee's mailing address before the county recorder will take it. Indiana Code 32-21-2-3 requires every recorded instrument to include an acknowledgment or a proof. A conveyance must also state the mailing address for tax statements and the grantee's own address, and that address must be a street address or a rural route address.

Recording costs are set by statute. Under IC 36-2-7-10 a deed or other instrument is $25 per recording and a mortgage is $55, with extra fees for oversized pages and copies. A county can add small fees by ordinance, such as an affordable housing fund charge of up to $10 per document where that applies.

Two more pieces sit alongside the deed:

  • Sales disclosure form. DLGF says the form is completed for a transfer of a real property interest for value made under a conveyance document. The transferor and transferee sign it. Mortgages, leases under ninety years, non-source-of-title quitclaim deeds and easements are excluded. The same form can also serve as an application for deductions such as the homestead deduction.
  • Auditor endorsement. For a property sold at tax sale and conveyed during its redemption period, the recorder may not record the conveyance document unless the county auditor has endorsed it.

Check with the recorder in your county for local formatting rules before you send anything, because counties publish their own checklists.

sections.h2: Does an Indiana seller have to give the buyer a disclosure form?
sections.html:
Yes for most residential sales, because Indiana Code 32-21-5 requires the owner to complete and sign a disclosure form and hand it to a prospective buyer before accepting an offer. The chapter covers sales, exchanges, installment sales contracts and lease-purchase deals for residential real estate with no more than four dwelling units.

The chapter lists exclusions. These include court-ordered transfers, transfers by a lender that took the property through foreclosure or a deed in lieu, transfers by a fiduciary managing an estate, guardianship or trust, transfers to a spouse or lineal descendant, transfers caused by unpaid taxes, and transfers to or from a government body. A first sale of a never-inhabited dwelling is also outside it.

An owner is not liable for an error that was outside the owner's actual knowledge, or that came from a public agency or a professional the owner reasonably believed to be correct, provided the owner was not negligent. Before closing, an accepted offer cannot be enforced against the buyer until both sides have signed the form. After closing, missing paperwork does not by itself undo the sale.

sections.h2: What problems do sellers in Indiana run into most?
sections.html:
Sellers usually face a handful of recurring situations, and Indiana law treats each one differently. The statewide guides on this site cover them one at a time, and these are the points that most often change a timeline:

  • Unpaid taxes. Bills come twice a year, and penalties of 5 and 10 percent stack on late installments.
  • Tenants in place. State law, not each city, governs most of the landlord-tenant relationship, and local governments cannot set rental rates, deposit rules or lease terms on their own.
  • Older homes. Houses financed by land contract in Indiana have a median construction year of 1952, which is 18 years older than the statewide median, according to Pew's 2026 analysis.
  • Inherited or court-controlled property. Fiduciary and court-ordered transfers sit outside the standard disclosure form, but the deed and recording steps still apply.
  • Seller-financed sales. Indiana recorded 31,431 land contracts from 2005 to 2024, the sixth-most of any state, even though it ranks 17th in population.

If one of those matches your house, read the matching state guide first and call a county office to confirm the current local steps.

faqs.q: How many counties does Indiana have?
faqs.a: Indiana has 92 counties. Marion County, home to Indianapolis, is the most populous, and Lake County is second. Each county has its own recorder, auditor, treasurer and assessor, so the office you call depends on where the house sits.

faqs.q: When are Indiana property taxes due?
faqs.a: Taxes are due in two installments each year, in May and on November 10. DLGF lists May 11 and November 10 for 2026. Late payment brings a 5 percent penalty within 30 days and 10 percent after that.

faqs.q: Who sends the property assessment notice in Indiana?
faqs.a: The county or township assessor mails the Form 11, which shows the assessed value of land and improvements. Some counties use the tax bill itself as the notice, so check with the assessor in your county.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in Indiana?
faqs.a: The statutory recording fee for a deed is $25 per recording under IC 36-2-7-10. Mortgages are $55, and a county may add small fees by ordinance. Ask the county recorder for the current total.

faqs.q: Does Indiana require a seller disclosure form?
faqs.a: Yes, for most residential sales of up to four units. The owner completes and signs the form and gives it to the buyer before accepting an offer. Estate fiduciaries, foreclosing lenders and several other transfers are excluded.

faqs.q: What is the 1 percent property tax cap in Indiana?
faqs.a: It is the circuit breaker cap for homestead property, which limits tax to 1 percent of gross assessed value. A property must receive the homestead standard deduction to qualify. Residential property that is not a homestead is capped at 2 percent.
